t: The LORD's name and the prophet's word
p: In this Plain the divine name YHWH is printed "the LORD"; "The word of the LORD that came to" opens four of the Twelve.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, which Jewish readers did not say aloud and which most English Bibles print as "the LORD" in capitals. This Plain does the same. "The word of the LORD that came to" is the opening of Hosea (Hosea 1:1), Joel (Joel 1:1), Micah and Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1), a stock heading for a prophet's collected message. Jonah opens almost the same way but tells a story. The heading says the book is a word received, not a speech composed, and the verb "came" (literally "was") treats the word as an event. Micah's book is mostly poetry, and this Plain sets it out in lines marked with " / ".

t: Micah, a man from the Shephelah
p: The prophet is named for his home town, a village in the lowland hills southwest of Jerusalem, near Gath.
b: Micah's name is a short form of Mikayahu, "Who is like the LORD?" The book ends on that question (7:18, in the other part of this book). Moresheth is Moresheth-gath (1:14), in the Shephelah, the low hills between the coastal plain and the mountains of Judah. It is usually placed at or near Tell el-Judeideh, not far from Gath and Mareshah. A man from a country town, not a court prophet, speaks against the capital. That fits his charges against the city's rulers (3:1-3, 9-12) but proves nothing about his rank. Jeremiah 26:18 calls him "Micah of Moresheth" and the written Hebrew text of that verse has the long name Mikayah, read aloud as Micah.

a: in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah
p: Micah spans about forty years of Judah's story, from the Syro-Ephraimite crisis through the Assyrian invasion.
b: Jotham (about 750 to 735 BC), Ahaz (about 735 to 715) and Hezekiah (about 715 to 686) are given in the dates most historians use; chronologies differ by several years (see regnal chronology). Their reigns cover the years when Assyria swallowed the north: Samaria fell in 722/721 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6; 2 Kings 18:9-12), and Sennacherib marched into Judah in 701 (2 Kings 18:13-17). Isaiah's heading names the same three kings and Uzziah before them (Isaiah 1:1). Only Hezekiah's reign is attested when Jeremiah's elders recall Micah (Jeremiah 26:18). Some critics think the heading was added later and that the book's material is not all from these years. Defenders of the heading note that its details (1:1, 1:6, 1:10-16) fit that period.

p: A prophet's "word" can be seen: the Hebrew verb is the one for a vision.
b: Hebrew says a prophet "saw" a word. The same verb opens Isaiah ("the word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw", Isaiah 2:1) and Amos ("the words of Amos... which he saw", Amos 1:1). The prophet is a "visionary" (chozeh, a term this Plain keeps apart from "seer", ro'eh). Here the grammar is plain: "which he saw" refers to the word of the LORD, and the word is "about Samaria and Jerusalem". Nothing in the book describes a visual scene, so "saw" here means "received", as it does in the headings of Isaiah and Amos. Micah later contrasts himself with the "visionaries" who will be ashamed (3:7).

p: The Hebrew Bible puts Micah sixth of the Twelve; the Greek Bible puts him third.
b: The Twelve Minor Prophets were copied as one scroll in Jewish tradition (Bava Batra 13b-15a). In the Hebrew order Micah follows Jonah and precedes Nahum: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk and on. The Greek order runs Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum. Both orders put the three 8th-century prophets of the north and south (Hosea, Amos, Micah) near the front, and some scholars read the order as shaped by catchwords and themes: Jonah 4:2 and Micah 7:18-20 (in the other part) both lean on Exodus 34:6-7, and Nahum 1:3 turns the same creed against Nineveh. Whether the Twelve was edited as one book is debated (Nogalski, Schart, Sweeney for; Ben Zvi and Barton against). See the topic The Book of the Twelve.

p: Micah is sent to Judah but names the northern capital first; the book keeps both in view.
b: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom, built by Omri (1 Kings 16:24). Jerusalem was the capital of Judah. Putting Samaria first fits an opening oracle about Samaria's fall (1:2-7), but the heading really names the two seats of power and religion whose guilt the book will compare (1:5). Isaiah says Assyria will do to Jerusalem what it did to Samaria (Isaiah 10:10-11). Micah's argument runs the other way: Samaria's ruin is the warning, and Judah's rulers have copied its sins (1:13; 3:9-12; 6:16 in the other part). Many scholars think the book was shaped to read as a whole in that order.

a: Hear this, peoples, every one of you.
p: The book is built in three rounds that each begin "Hear" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1); the peoples are called as witnesses.
b: Micah opens with a summons to all the peoples and the earth, as in a court. The same Hebrew words, shim'u 'ammim kullam, close the prophet Micaiah's warning to King Ahab, "Listen, peoples, all of you!" (1 Kings 22:28). That may be the writer's deliberate link between two prophets of almost the same name, or a later scribe's harmonizing; Swete's Greek text of 1 Kings 22:28 lacks the sentence, which leaves open that it entered the Hebrew of Kings from Micah. Each of the book's three parts begins "Hear" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) and moves from judgment to hope (2:12-13; 4:1-5:15; 7:7-20). The nations are summoned here to see what the LORD does to his own people; later they will stream to Zion (4:1-2). Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses the same way in Deuteronomy 32:1.
orig: שִׁמְעוּ עַמִּים כֻּלָּם (shim'u 'ammim kullam), 'hear, peoples, all of them'

a: Let the Lord GOD stand as a witness against you
t: Witness against you, or among you?
p: The small Hebrew word "in" can mean "against" or "among"; the court scene points to "against".
b: The Hebrew has ba-khem, literally "in you". English versions choose "against you" (as here) or "among you". The picture of a witness fits both: the LORD is the one who will testify, as in a courtroom (compare Malachi 3:5), and the testimony is what follows in 1:3-7. Calvin read "against you" and took the Lord's holy temple as heaven, from which he looks down (Psalm 11:4). The title "Lord GOD" (adonay YHWH) is this Plain's rendering of the double name, as in Amos 1:8.
orig: בָּכֶם לְעֵד (bakhem le'ed), 'in you, for a witness'

a: the Lord from his holy temple
p: The "holy temple" is either the Jerusalem Temple or God's heavenly palace.
b: Readers divide. Some take heikal qodsho as the Temple in Jerusalem, so that the judgment goes out from the very place whose rulers Micah will condemn (3:12). Others take it as the LORD's palace in heaven, as in Psalm 11:4, which puts the LORD in his holy temple and his throne in the heavens, and Habakkuk 2:20, and read the verse as a heavenly court summoning the earth. The next verse supports this: the LORD "comes down" from his place. Jewish and Christian commentators in the past mostly chose heaven; many modern ones hold that the Temple was understood as the earthly copy of the heavenly one, so both are meant.

p: Micah's picture of the LORD coming down and the mountains melting is older poetry about the LORD at Sinai and in battle.
b: God is pictured as a warrior-king leaving his place, and the earth reacts. The oldest examples are in Israel's early songs (Judges 5:4-5), where the LORD comes from Seir and the mountains "flow" before him. Psalm 18 pictures him coming down on a cherub through darkness (Psalm 18:7-15), and Habakkuk 3:3-6 and Nahum 1:3-5 use the same stock images. Amos opens with a similar roar from Zion (Amos 1:2). Here the setting is a lawsuit, not a battle: the warrior comes to testify and then to act. The image repeats in 1:3-4 for a reason: Samaria's guilt is not a human affair only (1:5-6).
r: Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 18:7-15; Psalm 97:5; Nahum 1:3-5; Habakkuk 3:3-6; Amos 1:2

p: "High places" is the ordinary word for hilltop shrines; here it is the earth's heights, and in 1:5 it names Jerusalem.
b: Bamot means "heights". In the Old Testament it is the standard word for the hilltop sanctuaries that Israel and Judah kept using, often with images and altars the prophets attacked. In 1:3 the LORD treads the earth's heights, as in Deuteronomy 32:13 and Amos 4:13, as a conqueror stepping on defeated ground. In 1:5 Micah turns the word on Jerusalem: "Who is behind Judah's high places?" Three verses apart, the heights of the earth are the LORD's footstool, and the heights of Judah are Jerusalem's sin. The Leningrad Codex and Mur88 spell the plural "heights" in 1:3 differently (the Codex without the vowel letter, Mur88 with it), a spelling difference with no effect on meaning. See the topic High places.

p: The mountains melt like wax and the valleys split: the picture is of the earth failing before the LORD.
b: Two images of the same event. Wax melts before fire, and water poured on a steep slope cannot be held. Psalm 97:5 says, "Like wax, the mountains melt away in the LORD's presence", and Psalm 68:2 says the wicked melt before God as wax before fire. Nahum 1:5 has mountains quaking and hills melting. Some commentators think the images come from volcanic eruption or earthquake; the poet only says that the ground gives way under the LORD's feet. In the book's own plot the melting mountains answer the people who trust in "the mountain of the house" (3:12): the mountains that will melt are the very ones the proud think safe. At the end, the mountain of the LORD's house is set "at the head of the mountains" (4:1).

p: The Hebrew asks "who" is Jacob's rebellion; the answer is a city, so the rebellion is traced to its capital.
b: Hebrew asks mi, "who?", and the answers are cities: Samaria, Jerusalem. English usually turns this into "what is Jacob's rebellion?" The sense is: who is the source, who is to blame? The question assigns the nation's sin to the seat of government and worship. The words for guilt are pesha' ("rebellion", the sin of breaking a bond) and chatta'ot ("sins"), kept apart in this Plain as in the Torah. "Jacob" and "Israel" name the northern kingdom here; in 3:1 and 3:8 they name the whole people, and the book moves between those two senses.
orig: מִי פֶשַׁע יַעֲקֹב (mi fesha' Ya'aqov), 'who is the rebellion of Jacob?'

t: What Samaria's fall did and did not do
p: Samaria fell to Assyria in 722/721 BC; the city was later rebuilt, so the poem's picture is a prophetic image, not a literal record.
b: Assyrian siege of Samaria began under Shalmaneser V and the city fell in 722/721 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6; 18:9-12); Sargon II claimed the victory and recorded deporting about 27,000 people. The exiles were resettled in Assyrian lands and foreigners were brought in (2 Kings 17:24). The city itself was reoccupied and flourished as an Assyrian provincial capital; later Hellenistic and Roman cities (Sebaste) stood on the site. So the "ruin-heap" and "vines" are prophetic pictures: the city loses its power and wealth and becomes farmland. Dating is disputed. A prediction before 722 puts Micah in Ahaz's reign or earlier; some critics think the oracle looks back on the fall. Readings of the fulfillment differ only in how literally "ruin-heap" is taken.
orig: לְעִי הַשָּׂדֶה (le'i hassadeh), 'a heap of the field'

p: Three words for idols: carved images, wages, and idols.
b: Pesilim are carved images, a term that the second commandment's "carved image" (Exodus 20:4) also uses; 'atsabbim are idols, a word Hosea also uses (Hosea 4:17; 8:4). Micah lists three things to be destroyed: images to be beaten into pieces, "wages" to go up in fire, idols to become a wasteland. The northern kingdom, whose kings set up calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-30) and whose people followed the Baals, was known for its images (Hosea 8:5-6; 10:5-6). Two of the Dead Sea scrolls preserve this verse, 4Q82 (4QXIIg) and Mur88, and both agree with the Masoretic Text.

a: She gathered them from a prostitute's pay
p: Samaria's wealth is called a prostitute's fee; the picture is Hosea's, and the fee returns to its kind.
b: The Hebrew word 'etnan means a prostitute's payment, "hire". Hosea uses it of Israel's idolatrous prosperity: "You have loved the pay of a prostitute on every threshing floor of grain" (Hosea 9:1), and the Plain keeps "prostitute" for zonah throughout the Twelve (see the term in Hosea). Micah's image is: the idol-silver and gold of Samaria were gained, as the people thought, from false gods; the wealth gained as hire will become hire again in the hands of others (one proposal names foreign temples or soldiers; the verse does not). Ancient commentators and some moderns read it literally of temple prostitution; the debate about whether such a practice existed is discussed at Hosea 4:14. Others read the whole phrase as a metaphor for covenant unfaithfulness. The verse's last line is a proverb-like turn: what is gained one way is lost the same way.
orig: מֵאֶתְנַן זוֹנָה (me'etnan zonah), 'from a prostitute's hire'

a: That is why I will mourn and howl.
p: The one who walks barefoot and howls is the prophet, or the LORD, or Judah personified.
b: Verse 8 begins "On this I will lament", and the Hebrew gives no name. The usual reading is that Micah himself mourns, acting out grief with bare feet and stripped clothes (like Isaiah's walking naked and barefoot for three years, Isaiah 20:2-4). Some ancient and some modern commentators hear the LORD grieving over his people, in the way Jeremiah hears God's grief (Jeremiah 9:10; 48:31). A third view makes the speaker Judah or Jerusalem, as in the poems of Lamentations. The grief is real either way: the prophet who announces judgment shares the pain of it. Mourning customs here include going barefoot, taking off ornaments and calling out like wild animals at night.

p: The two animals are known for loud night cries; the Greek turns them into "dragons" and "sirens".
b: The Hebrew tannim (usually read as jackals) and bat ya'anah ("daughter of the ostrich", ostriches or possibly owls) are animals of ruins and wasteland whose cries sound like weeping (Job 30:29). Isaiah pictures them in Babylon's ruins (Isaiah 13:21-22). The Greek translator reads "dragons" and "daughters of sirens" for the same words (Swete's text), a choice that tells more about Greek legends than about Micah. Whichever animal, the prophet will make a noise that cannot be mistaken for a speech.

p: The blow that fell on Samaria now "touches" the gate of Jerusalem: this fits Assyria's march into Judah, usually dated 701 BC.
b: "Incurable" ('anushah) is the same word Jeremiah uses of his own wound (Jeremiah 15:18) and of Judah's (Jeremiah 30:12). The wound is Samaria's fall, and the verse says it has spread: "to Judah... to the gate of my people." The "gate" is where a city's elders sat in judgment and where its defenders stood. Isaiah describes the same event as a flood reaching the neck of Judah (Isaiah 8:7-8). Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC reached the walls of Jerusalem after taking many Judean towns (2 Kings 18:13-19:36). The tradition that this is the same event as the town list in 1:10-16 is the common one.

p: The line quotes David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, with a pun on "tell".
b: Micah 1:10-16 is a run of puns on the names of towns in the Shephelah. This line begins it with a quotation: "Do not tell it in Gath" (2 Samuel 1:20), where David asks that the Philistines in Gath not hear that Saul and Jonathan are dead. In Hebrew "tell" (taggidu) sounds like "Gath" (Gat). Micah turns David's words around: now it is Judah's fall that must be kept from Gath, because Israel's enemies would gloat. Micah's own village was Moresheth-gath (1:14), so the prophet is naming his neighbors. The Plain's wording is David's, because the Hebrew words are the same, in a different order ("in Gath do not tell" here, "do not tell it in Gath" in 2 Samuel 1:20).
orig: בְּגַת אַל־תַּגִּידוּ (begat 'al-taggidu), 'in Gath do not tell'

p: Beth-leaphrah means "house of dust", and the verse has the Hebrew word for dust twice.
b: Beth-le'afrah is "house of dust" (Hebrew 'afar, "dust"). The verse says: in the house of dust, roll in the dust, a sound-play the Plain keeps by leaving the name in Hebrew and giving the meaning in the gloss. Rolling in dust and ashes is a sign of mourning (Jeremiah 6:26; Ezekiel 27:30). The place cannot be identified with confidence. Its identification is uncertain; the name appears nowhere else.
orig: בֵּית לְעַפְרָה עָפָר (bet le'afrah 'afar), 'in Beth-le-Aphrah, dust'

p: Shaphir sounds like the word for "pleasant"; the people of the "Pleasant" town leave in shame.
b: Shapir (Shaphir) means "pleasant" or "fair". The poet's irony is plain: the town called Pleasant leaves in nakedness and shame, as prisoners of war were led away with their clothes stripped (Isaiah 20:4). The place is unknown. The Hebrew says "nakedness, shame" side by side ('eryah-boshet), a pair some translate as "naked and in shame" and others read as "in shameful nakedness". The Greek reads Shaphir as an adverb, "beautifully" (Swete).

p: Zaanan sounds like the Hebrew "go out"; the people of "Go-out-town" cannot go out.
b: Tsa'anan (probably the Zenan of Joshua 15:37, in the Shephelah) plays on yatsa'ah, "she went out". The people of Zaanan do not come out: the town is under siege, or too afraid to move. It echoes the way city gates and siege are described in Jeremiah ("the one who goes out to the field... the one who enters the city", Jeremiah 14:18). Rhymes like this cannot be reproduced in English without losing the real names, so the Plain keeps the names and teaches the sound in the gloss.
orig: לֹא יָצְאָה יוֹשֶׁבֶת צַאֲנָן (lo yatse'ah yoshevet Tsa'anan)

p: The Hebrew of the last two lines is very hard; the Plain follows a common reading of "standing ground".
b: Beth-ha'etsel (Beth-ezel) is probably "house of the side" or "next-door house". The Hebrew is hard: mispad Beth ha'etsel yiqqach mikkem 'omdato, "the lament of Beth-ezel takes from you its standing place". Readings: (1) the mourning of Beth-ezel removes its (own) support from you, meaning the neighbor town offers no refuge (the Plain's sense); (2) Beth-ezel (the "next-door house") mourns and "takes its stand" away from you; (3) with a different word division, "its fortress is taken from you". The noun 'omdah appears only here. The Greek reads "she will take from you a painful blow" (Swete), a very different sense. Beth-ezel is unidentified; Zechariah 14:5 has a similar word (Atsal) for a place near Jerusalem.
orig: בֵּית הָאֵצֶל (bet ha'etsel), 'Beth-ha-ezel, house of the side'

t: Maroth, the town of bitter things
p: Maroth means "bitter things"; its people hope for good but get disaster from the LORD.
b: Marot is the plural of "bitter" (compare Marah, "bitter", Exodus 15:23). The people there "ache" or "writhe" (chalah, usually "to be sick" or "in labor") for good, or "wait" for it (some link the verb to yachal, "to wait"). The Hebrew pun is: the people of Bitter-town hope for sweetness and get what the name says. The cause is stated plainly: disaster has come down "from the LORD" to the very gate of Jerusalem. This is the only line in the section that names who is behind all the puns. Maroth is unidentified; some link it to Maarath (Joshua 15:59).

p: Lachish was Judah's chief fortress in the Shephelah and Sennacherib's headquarters in 701 BC.
b: Lachish (Tell ed-Duweir) was Judah's chief fortress after Jerusalem, a city Rehoboam fortified (2 Chronicles 11:9). Sennacherib besieged and took it in 701 BC; his palace at Nineveh was decorated with a long relief showing the assault, now in the British Museum, and Ussishkin's excavations found the Assyrian siege ramp and a layer of destruction. 2 Kings 18:14 and 18:17 place Sennacherib's camp there while Hezekiah paid tribute: "Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish" (2 Kings 18:14). The Hebrew pun is rekesh, "team of swift horses", and Lakish: Micah says to harness the team to flee. Sennacherib's own account (the Taylor Prism, in the British Museum) says he took 46 walled Judean cities and deported 200,150 people, with Hezekiah shut up "like a bird in a cage".
orig: לָכִישׁ (Lakhish) and לָרֶכֶשׁ (larekhesh), 'to the team of horses'

a: You were the start of sin for Daughter Zion
p: Three views: horses and chariots (military trust), Lachish as the road for idolatry from the north, or a general charge.
b: Reshit chatta't hi, "she is the beginning of sin". What sin? (1) Trust in horses and chariots instead of the LORD: Lachish was a fortified city (2 Chronicles 11:9), and the verse's horses and chariot may point to its military role; Isaiah condemns those who rely on "horses" and "chariots" (Isaiah 31:1; Deuteronomy 17:16). The verse puts the order to harness the chariot right before the charge. (2) The place where Samaria's idolatry first crossed into Judah; the text calls it "Israel's rebellions" (also 1:5). (3) A general indictment of a town that led others. The phrase "Daughter Zion" (bat Tsiyyon) first appears in Micah here (Isaiah 1:8 uses it earlier in the canon) and is used as the name of Jerusalem and its people in 4:8, 10, 13, as in Isaiah and Lamentations.

p: The word is used for a dowry or gift sent with a daughter who leaves home; Moresheth-gath is given away.
b: Shilluchim are things "sent away", and the word is used of a bride's parting gifts: Pharaoh gave Gezer as shilluchim to his daughter when she became Solomon's wife (1 Kings 9:16). The sense here is that Daughter Zion will hand over Moresheth-gath, Micah's own town, as one gives up a daughter. There is also a sound-play on Moresheth and me'orasah, "betrothed". The Greek translator reads the line differently: "he will give those sent away as far as the inheritance of Gath" (Swete).
orig: שִׁלּוּחִים עַל מוֹרֶשֶׁת גַּת (shilluchim 'al Moreshet Gat)

p: Achzib sounds like the Hebrew for "deceptive"; a stream that fails in the dry season is the picture.
b: Akhziv (Achzib; the place is in the Shephelah, Joshua 15:44) is near the Hebrew akhzav, "deceptive". The word is used of a seasonal stream that disappears in summer: Jeremiah says the LORD has become to him "like something that deceives, like waters that cannot be trusted" (Jeremiah 15:18). So the houses of Achzib will fail the kings of Israel as a dry streambed fails the traveler. "The kings of Israel" here are probably the kings of Judah (the name "Israel" is often used for the whole people in Micah), who counted on the fortress towns.
orig: אַכְזִיב לְאַכְזָב (Akhziv le'akhzav), 'Achzib for a deception'

p: Mareshah sounds like the Hebrew "one who takes possession" (heir or conqueror).
b: Mareshah (Tell Sandahannah/Maresha, in the Shephelah; fortified under Rehoboam, 2 Chronicles 11:8) resembles yoresh, "the one who takes possession" (also "heir"). The poem warns that a dispossessor will come to the town named for possession. In other Old Testament uses the same verb describes a conqueror taking a land. Who is the one who takes possession? The Assyrian king (the usual view), or God's agent. The Greek renders "heirs" (Swete), which reads the name as a common word.
orig: הַיֹּרֵשׁ אָבִיא לָךְ יוֹשֶׁבֶת מָרֵשָׁה (hayyoresh 'avi lakh yoshevet Mareshah)

p: Adullam is where David hid; the "glory of Israel" may be the nobles who flee there.
b: Adullam is the cave where David hid from Saul, and where his family and the discontented joined him: "David got away from there and fled to the cave of Adullam" (1 Samuel 22:1). The "glory of Israel" is either Judah's nobles (compare Isaiah 5:13, "its glory"), who will end up like David the outlaw, or the LORD's own glory going into the wilderness as it did when David fled. Some read this line as hope: as David came out of Adullam to be king, so a new leader (compare 5:2) comes from hiding. The Plain keeps the plain grammar: "will come as far as Adullam".

p: The Hebrew nesher is the large griffon vulture, whose head is bald.
b: Nesher is traditionally "eagle", but here the point is baldness, and the griffon vulture is pale-headed with a thin covering of down. Mourners shaved their heads (Job 1:20; Amos 8:10; Jeremiah 7:29). The call is to the "daughter" (the unnamed town of the verse), telling her to cut off her hair in grief for her children. The reason is exile: "for they will be taken from you into exile". The Assyrians' practice of mass deportation is documented in their annals and on their reliefs, and Sennacherib claims 200,150 people from Judah in 701 BC (the Taylor Prism).

a: Woe to those who plan trouble
p: "Woe" (hoy) was first the cry at a funeral; Micah speaks of the powerful as already dead.
b: Hoy is the cry people made at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30 has it as "Alas, my brother"). Prophets use it to open a threat, as in Isaiah 5:8, 11, 18, 20, 21, 22. This Plain reads it as "Woe to" before the people addressed. It is a sharp opening: the people described here are still alive and busy, but the prophet already mourns them. The sin begins in the night: they "plan" (chashav) and "work out" evil on their beds, then carry it out at dawn. The LORD answers with the same verb in 2:3: "I am planning" a disaster against them.
orig: הוֹי חֹשְׁבֵי־אָוֶן (hoy chosheve 'aven), 'woe, planners of trouble'

a: since their hands are strong enough
p: A Hebrew idiom for "they can"; some hear "their hand is their god" instead.
b: The Hebrew is yesh le'el yadam, "there is to the power ('el) of their hand". The idiom appears elsewhere: Jacob's father-in-law says it was in the power of his hand to do Jacob harm (Genesis 31:29); Proverbs 3:27 says not to hold back good when it is in the power of your hand to do it; and in the negative, Deuteronomy 28:32 says there will be nothing in the power of your hand. So the line says the rich plan such acts because they have the means. A few commentators have read 'el as "God", so that "their hand is their god" (compare Habakkuk 1:11), power as an idol. The Plain follows the idiom. The point is the same either way: they do wrong because nothing stops them.

a: They crave fields and grab them.
p: The verb is the one in the tenth commandment; Micah shows craving that becomes action.
b: The Hebrew verb chamad is the one in the last of the Ten Commandments: "You must not crave your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:17). Micah's picture is the next step: they crave a field, then seize it. The phrase "field... house" echoes the law about boundaries (Deuteronomy 19:14) and Isaiah's woe: "Woe to those who string house onto house and attach field to field" (Isaiah 5:8). Jewish tradition asks whether "do not crave" is about the heart or the deed; Micah answers by joining craving and seizing in one line. Naboth's vineyard shows how a king's craving was carried out by a court (1 Kings 21).
orig: וְחָמְדוּ שָׂדוֹת וְגָזָלוּ (vechamedu sadot vegazalu), 'they craved fields and seized'

t: Family land and the LORD's land
p: In Israel's law the land belonged to the LORD and could not be sold for good; seizing a family plot attacked that order.
b: The Hebrew nachalah, "inheritance", is the family's share of the land given at the conquest. The law says: "The land must not be sold for good, because the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23), and "An inheritance of the Israelites must not move from one tribe to another" (Numbers 36:7). When Ahab asked for Naboth's vineyard, the answer was "The LORD keep me from giving you my fathers' inheritance!" (1 Kings 21:3). In Micah's day debt, forced sale and royal land grants were putting plots into the hands of a few officials. The prophet sees these as thefts committed by people with legal tools. The text does not name the men; commentators think of officials and wealthy landowners.

a: I am planning a disaster against this clan
p: The verb "plan" returns: the planners are answered by the LORD's plan.
b: Chashav "plan" is used of the rich in 2:1 and of the LORD here, in the same grammar: they plan trouble in bed, he plans a disaster against them. Ra'ah means both "evil" and "disaster"; this Plain uses "evil" for what people do and "disaster" for what God sends, and keeps the link in notes, as it does in Jonah. "Clan" (mishpachah) is the whole extended family, the nation viewed as one house; Amos uses the word the same way (Amos 3:1). The "necks" are a picture of a yoke they cannot slip. "Heads held high" is a rare word (romah), "haughtily".
orig: הִנְנִי חֹשֵׁב עַל־הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה הַזֹּאת רָעָה (hinni choshev 'al-hammishpachah hazzo't ra'ah)

t: "The LORD says this": a messenger's words
p: The Hebrew koh amar YHWH is the formula of a messenger delivering a king's words.
b: The Hebrew koh amar YHWH ("thus says the LORD") is the formula of a messenger who brings the words of the one who sent him. In ordinary use it opens a message from a master: Jacob's servants say "Thus says your servant Jacob" to Esau (Genesis 32:4), and the Assyrian field commander says "Thus says the great king" to Hezekiah's officials (2 Kings 18:19). The prophets use it of the LORD, so that the prophet stands as his messenger and not as the author of the words. This Plain renders it "The LORD says this" throughout (as in Samuel and Kings). It first appears in Micah here, and again in 3:5.
orig: כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה (koh amar YHWH), 'thus says the LORD'

t: A taunt song and a funeral song
p: The "taunt" (mashal) is a mocking song; the next words are the mockery, a dirge sung back at the rich.
b: A mashal is a short poem, proverb or saying; in a context like this (Isaiah 14:4; Habakkuk 2:6) it is a mocking song against a fallen enemy. The "mournful dirge" is a play on sound (nahah nehi nihyah), a hard phrase whose second and third words are rare. The song that follows, "We are completely ruined!", is probably what the dispossessed or an onlooker will sing in the voice of the ruined landowners, quoting them back. So the oppressors will be taunted with their own cry. Who "he" is, in "He trades away my people's share", is the LORD (the Plain's reading) or the new owner, an invader.
orig: וְנָהָה נְהִי נִהְיָה (venahah nehi nihyah), 'and he will wail a wailing'

p: The Hebrew shovev is "one who turns away": a traitor, an unfaithful person, or a conqueror.
b: The ending of the song is hard: leshovev sadenu yechalleq, "to the one who turns away our fields he divides". Shovev means one who turns away or back. It is a favorite word of Jeremiah for faithless Israel (Jeremiah 3:14, 22; 31:22). Possible readings: the "traitor" is the new owner, an Israelite who has turned from God; the conqueror; or the whole phrase means "fields that will be divided among those who turn away from us". Another proposal changes one letter to read "the captor". The Greek reads a different sentence altogether (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Hebrew word and the most common sense, "traitor".

a: stretch a measuring line for you by lot
t: No one to cast the lot
p: The land was divided by lot in Joshua; the verse says the oppressors' families will have no share in the next division.
b: Israel's land was first shared out by lot at Shiloh, with measuring cords: "Then I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God" (Joshua 18:6). Numbers 26:55 says the land is to be divided by lot among the tribes. The threat is that no one will measure out a share for these families in "the LORD's assembly" (qehal YHWH), the people as a congregation (Deuteronomy 23:1-8). Two readings: (1) in the coming exile the land will be divided by others and the powerful will have no new portion; (2) in the future restoration there will be a new allotment (compare Ezekiel 47:13-14), and the greedy will be left out. Both agree: those who took land for themselves lose their place in the shared inheritance.

p: The Hebrew verb for "rant" literally means "drip"; Micah's opponents use it with contempt, as Amaziah does to Amos.
b: The verb natap means "drip" and is used of speech: Job 29:22 (my words "dripped" on them), Proverbs 5:3. Amaziah uses it against Amos: "Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not rant against the house of Isaac" (Amos 7:16). The Plain says "rant" here to match Amos, since the speakers in both places use the word as a sneer. In Micah the sneer becomes a play: the same word returns in 2:11 as the "ranter" who talks about wine, a word that also means what mountains "drip" (Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13). The first speakers are the opponents, answered by Micah (2:7); who they are, powerful landowners or fellow prophets, is not stated. The Greek reads "weep" (see the variant).
orig: אַל־תַּטִּיפוּ יַטִּיפוּן (al-tattifu yattifun), 'do not drip, they drip'

a: Shame will not be turned back.
p: The Hebrew is five hard words; three readings give three speakers.
b: Lo yissag kelimmot: "shame will not be turned back." The verb means to be moved back or removed, the noun is a plural, "disgraces". Readings: (1) the opponents say, "Disgrace will not overtake us", a boast that the threatened shame will not come; (2) Micah (or the LORD) says that the shame will not be turned back, it cannot be averted; (3) with a small change, "they will not turn away from shame", the speaker says the insults will not stop. The Plain keeps the plain wording, which can bear (1) or (2) depending on who speaks. The next verse is the prophet's answer.

a: Is the LORD's Spirit cut short?
p: "Short of spirit" means impatient or weak; the question asks whether the LORD has lost patience or power.
b: Ruach means spirit, breath and wind, and in a short phrase also patience. Exodus 6:9 says the people did not listen to Moses "from shortness of spirit"; Numbers 21:4 says the people's spirit was "cut short" on the road; Job 21:4 asks why his spirit should not be short. So the question in Micah asks whether the LORD is short-tempered, impatient, or weak. The opponents say the LORD cannot be so harsh as to punish his people; Micah's answer is that his words do good "for the one who walks straight". The Spirit also comes back in 3:8, where Micah says the Spirit is with him. Note the sound play: in 2:11 ruach is the "wind" the lying prophet is full of.

a: Only yesterday my people rose up to be an enemy.
p: The first line changes from the LORD speaking of "my people" to the rich who treat the poor as enemies.
b: Verses 8-9 are hard Hebrew. The first line can be read: "Only yesterday my people rose up as an enemy" (they turned against the LORD, or the powerful turn against their own people), or with a small change, "my people are raising themselves against..." The Greek reads "in front... my people stood up in enmity". The Plain keeps the Hebrew order: the change is recent, "yesterday". The next lines describe what the rich do: they pull off "the fine cloak" ('adderet) from over the robe of passers-by who feel safe, men coming back from war. Soldiers coming home are the last people anyone expects to be robbed.
orig: וְאֶתְמוֹל עַמִּי לְאוֹיֵב יְקוֹמֵם (ve'etmol 'ammi le'oyev yeqomem)

a: out of the houses they love
p: The victims are women and children, whose homes and family land are taken when a husband dies.
b: "The women of my people" are probably widows: when the head of a household died or was taken in debt, his widow and children lost the house and the land. Law and prophets name widows and orphans as the ones to be protected (Exodus 22:22-24; Isaiah 1:17, 23; 10:2). The line "from the house of her delights" says what is taken from them: not just shelter but pleasant things. And from their children the powerful take "my honor" (hadari), the dignity God had given them. The ancient reader had no social welfare; to lose the family plot meant dependence or debt slavery (2 Kings 4:1).
orig: מִבֵּית תַּעֲנֻגֶיהָ (mibbet ta'anugeha), 'from the house of her delights'

p: Hadari: the dignity God gives; commentators take it as the image of God, God's blessing, or the child's place in the land.
b: Hadar means majesty, splendor, honor; of kings and of God (Psalm 8:5; 104:1). Taking "my honor" from children has been read: as the dignity the LORD gave them as members of his people, the land and name; as God's own honor, since to ruin his people's children is to damage his reputation (Ezekiel 36:20); or, as the writer's own association (no commentary cited here proposes it), the image of God (Genesis 1:27) in the poor. The idea in all of them: what is done to the weak is done to God's honor.

p: The "resting place" is the land God promised; here God tells his people to leave it.
b: In Deuteronomy the land is "the resting place and the inheritance" (Deuteronomy 12:9), and Psalm 95:11 warns of those who will not enter God's "rest". The word is menuchah. Micah turns it over: it is the people themselves who have made the place unclean (tame'), the way Leviticus warns that the land will "vomit out" its people (Leviticus 18:24-28; 20:22). The command "Get up and go!" is God's order to go into exile. What the land cannot bear is injustice, not only idolatry. The Plain's "It will ruin you" follows the Hebrew, a play on chavel: "it ruins, with a painful ruin".

a: full of wind and told lies
p: The popular prophet the people want is full of wind and talks about wine and beer.
b: The line is bitter satire. Ruach is wind or spirit; a man who "walks in wind and lies" is the opposite of one who has the LORD's Spirit (3:8). The people do not want Micah's message. They want a ranter who will promise them wine and beer: a prophet of plenty. Isaiah shows what it looks like when priests and prophets reel with beer (Isaiah 28:7). The verb "rant" (natap, "drip") and the word for wine hint at what the mountains "drip" in the age of plenty (Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13), so the satire turns the hope of abundance against those who make it a slogan. Beer is the grain drink of the ancient Near East (see Isaiah 5:11, 22).
orig: הֹלֵךְ רוּחַ וְשֶׁקֶר כִּזֵּב (holekh ruach vesheqer kizzev)

p: The Hebrew sheerit is the "remnant": the survivors, small but not lost; Micah returns to the idea at 4:7; 5:7-8 and 7:18.
b: She'erit means what is left over. In the prophets it is both a threat (only a few will survive) and a promise (God will keep a core). Isaiah named a son Shear-jashub, "A remnant will return" (Isaiah 7:3). Micah's remnant verses are 2:12, 4:7, 5:7-8 and 7:18, and they mark the book's hopeful turns. Here the LORD himself gathers them, twice over in the Hebrew: "I will surely gather... I will surely bring together". The word for gather, asaf, is the same used in 4:6 and 4:11. See the topic The Remnant.

a: The place will be loud with people.
p: The sheepfold is crowded and noisy: a picture of a restored people, not of panic.
b: Tehimenah me'adam means they will "hum" or "make a noise" from people (from the crowd of humans). The verb is about commotion, as in a crowded city (1 Kings 1:45, where the city is in an uproar). In a fold it is the noise of many sheep. It is a joyful sound in the salvation reading and a panicked one in the judgment reading (a besieged city full of refugees). In the Greek the sheep are "in distress" (see the variant).

p: The breaker (happorets) goes ahead of the flock; he is God, a Davidic king, or an unnamed leader, and the verses are salvation or judgment.
b: Happorets, "the one who breaks through", opens the way ahead of the flock, through the gate, with the king and the LORD behind. Readings: (1) The verses promise the return of the exiles with the LORD leading as shepherd-king (the view of many modern commentators). Jerome is reported in later commentaries to have read the "breaker" as Christ going before his people (not checked in his own commentary). (2) The breaker is the LORD himself, and "king" and "LORD" in the last lines are two names for one leader. (3) A minority reads 2:12-13 as judgment: the people are penned like sheep in a besieged city, and the breaker is the enemy or the LORD breaking down the wall (no commentator is named here; the Greek "in distress" at 2:12 supports it). The Greek of 2:13 has no person at all (see the variant). Rashi, Radak and the Targum comment here; their wording has not been checked, so no Jewish reading is reported. Many scholars think 2:12-13 may have been added after Micah's day, as an exilic hope (commentators such as Wolff and Mays); others defend it as Micah's own (Waltke). The name of the breaker recalls Perez (Genesis 38:29), "breach", and David's Baal-perazim (2 Samuel 5:20).

a: the LORD walks at their head
p: The LORD at the head of the people recalls the pillar in the exodus and Isaiah's new exodus.
b: At the exodus the LORD went before the people in a pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21). Isaiah promises the same at the return from exile: "the LORD will go ahead of you, and the God of Israel will guard your rear" (Isaiah 52:12). In Micah the leader is shepherd and king (compare 5:4), and the LORD's place "at their head" is the place of the commander (compare the term rosh, "head", for leader in 3:1). The picture of a flock led through a gate out of a place of danger makes this verse one of the book's clearest exodus images.

a: Hear this, you who head Jacob
p: Chapter 3 begins the book's second round ("Hear"); the first speech was to the nations, this one to the rulers.
b: Shim'u na, "Hear, please", opens the second of the book's three "Hear" speeches (1:2; 3:1; 6:1). The audience narrows from "peoples" (1:2) to the "heads of Jacob" and "rulers of the house of Israel": the officials who judge and govern. The Hebrew words are rashim ("heads") and qetsinim ("rulers", also used for Sodom's leaders in Isaiah 1:10). "And I said" marks Micah speaking in his own voice after the LORD's speech in chapter 2. In 3:9 the same words open a second address to the same men.

a: Should you not be the ones who know justice?
p: Mishpat (justice) is what officials were meant to know and keep; the next verses show them doing the reverse.
b: Mishpat means decision, ruling, judgment and, in the prophets, justice: what is right in a court and in a society. The king is to do mishpat (2 Samuel 8:15; Psalm 72:1-4). Micah asks: is it not your job to know it? The question is sharp because the rulers do know it (3:9, "abhor justice"). It is the prophet who is full of it (3:8). Micah uses the word with Isaiah (Isaiah 1:17, 21) and Amos (Amos 5:24); the Plain keeps "justice" for mishpat and "righteousness" for tsedaqah.
orig: הֲלוֹא לָכֶם לָדַעַת אֶת־הַמִּשְׁפָּט (halo lakhem lada'at et-hammishpat)

a: You hate good and love evil.
p: Amos says to hate evil and love good; Micah says the rulers have done the opposite.
b: Amos 5:15 gives the call: "Hate what is evil and love what is good. Make justice stand firm at the gate." Micah says the rulers have done the opposite, as Isaiah says that some call evil good and good evil (Isaiah 5:20). The scroll Mur88 writes the word for "evil" with a final he (ra'ah), the other spelling, which makes no difference to the sense. The brutal verbs that follow ("rip... off") are not about food yet; they build to the cooking pot of verse 3.

a: You eat the flesh of my people.
p: Rulers who strip the poor are pictured as butchers and cannibals; Ezekiel and the Psalms use the same picture.
b: The images are of butchering and cooking. Verse 2 flays, verse 3 eats and boils. Elsewhere the language is also used: wicked people "devour my people as they would eat bread" (Psalm 14:4), and Ezekiel describes the leaders of Jerusalem who say "This city is the pot, and we are the meat" (Ezekiel 11:3; compare Ezekiel 24:3-5). Zephaniah calls officials lions and judges wolves (Zephaniah 3:3). The picture is figurative. The picture says what taxes, forced sales and false judgments do: they take a person's living, skin and bones, and leave nothing. The same picture, in the mouth of "my people", says it is God who is the victim.

p: The verb after "break" is the usual word for "spread out"; here it must mean "cut up" or "chop up".
b: Ufarsu comes from paras ("spread out, break apart"). The Greek translator has "dismembered", and most English versions render "chop up". The Hebrew of the line is said to be corrupt by some (it may have lost a word), but the sense is clear from the cooking pot and cauldron that follow. The scroll Mur88 has this word, ufarsu, as the Masoretic Text does. The cauldron (qallachat) is the large pot of the kitchen, found in the story of Samuel's boiled meat (1 Samuel 2:14).

t: When the LORD does not answer
p: The people who never listened to the LORD's call for justice will cry and not be heard.
b: A consistent teaching in the Bible: those who stop their ears to the poor find that God stops his to them. Proverbs 1:28 has the LORD say, "Then they will call me, and I will give no answer." Isaiah 1:15 says he will not hear their prayers when "blood fills your hands". God "hides his face" in Deuteronomy 31:17-18 as a sign of a broken covenant. In Micah it applies to the rulers, not the poor. The poor who cry out are heard (Exodus 22:23); the rulers who cry out are not.

p: Prophets who say "Peace" to those who pay them are a theme of Jeremiah and Ezekiel too; the test is whether the message fits the facts.
b: Micah's charge is that some prophets tailor the message to their pay. Jeremiah quotes the same cry: "Peace, peace," when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 8:11), and Ezekiel says they "led my people astray, saying, 'Peace!' when there is no peace" (Ezekiel 13:10). The test of a true prophet in Deuteronomy is that the word comes true (Deuteronomy 18:22); in Micah the test is who is paid. The text does not call these men unbelievers. They bear the title "prophet" and they proclaim peace in the LORD's name (compare 3:11). See the topic False prophets.

a: They bite with their teeth and shout, "Peace!"
p: The prophets who are fed say "Peace"; those who are not fed get a "holy war", literally war they have sanctified.
b: The Hebrew nashak is "bite", also the word for charging interest, which "bites" (it is the root of neshek, interest; Deuteronomy 23:19-20). The prophets "bite with their teeth", meaning they have food to chew, and cry "Peace" (shalom); but if someone puts nothing in their mouths, they "consecrate war" (qiddeshu milchamah), a phrase for the religious rites that opened a campaign (Jeremiah 6:4; Joel 3:9, "declare holy war"). The point is that their words depend on payment. For other uses of the same expression, see the topic Holy war.
orig: וְקִדְּשׁוּ עָלָיו מִלְחָמָה (veqiddeshu 'alav milchamah), 'they consecrate war against him'

p: Night and darkness fall on the prophets: they will get no vision, no answer.
b: "Night" and "darkness" are the loss of revelation. Isaiah 8:19-22 warns of consulting mediums and ends in "gloom and darkness". Amos 8:9, "I will make the sun set at midday", is the same picture. The Hebrew also says "the sun will go (down) on the prophets", a plain picture of the day ending for them. In the book's pattern, the prophets who sold light are left with none. Lamentations 2:9 later sees the result: her prophets find no vision from the LORD.

p: Covering the upper lip is a sign of mourning and shame; Leviticus and Ezekiel have it.
b: The Hebrew says "cover the mustache" (sapham, upper lip). A person with a skin disease was to cover the upper lip and cry "Unclean" (Leviticus 13:45), and Ezekiel is told not to follow the usual mourning customs, which include covering the lip (Ezekiel 24:17, 22). The gesture means: I have no answer, I cannot speak. It is fitting for visionaries (chozim) and diviners (qosemim) with no answer from God. The word for diviner is the one condemned in the law (Deuteronomy 18:10, 14); Micah applies it to those who, like the diviners, sell their readings.

a: the LORD's Spirit is with me
p: Micah says his power, justice and strength come from the LORD's Spirit: rare in the 8th-century prophets.
b: Most prophets before the exile do not say the Spirit empowers them; Hosea's "man of the spirit" is called mad by his critics (Hosea 9:7). Micah says the opposite: the Spirit is with him, with justice and might, so that he can name Israel's guilt. This verse is the contrast to the "wind" of the lying prophet (2:11). Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets with the LORD's spirit (Numbers 11:29) is behind it. Some scholars since Wellhausen have thought the words "with the Spirit of the LORD" were added to the Hebrew by a later hand; no manuscript lacks them, and Mur88 has them. The Greek reads "in the Spirit of the LORD" (see the variant).

p: Habakkuk and Jeremiah use almost the same words against building by violence and unpaid labor.
b: "Woe to the one who builds a city with bloodshed" is Habakkuk 2:12, and Jeremiah's "Woe to the man who builds his house without righteousness... who has his fellow citizen work for nothing" (Jeremiah 22:13) names the method. Jerusalem was growing in Micah's day, and Hezekiah's walls and water tunnel were large projects (2 Kings 20:20). The text does not say which building Micah means, and Jeremiah's woe shows how building could rest on unpaid labor. The "blood" may be literal (murder, judicial killing, 3:3) or the price of life. The Hebrew uses the plural "bloods" (damim), the ordinary word for bloodshed. See the topics Justice and Mount Zion.

p: Each of the three offices takes pay: judges a bribe, priests a fee, prophets silver.
b: Shochad is a bribe, a gift to a judge that bends his ruling. The law forbids it flatly: "Do not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see clearly and turns the words of the righteous upside down" (Exodus 23:8; compare Deuteronomy 16:19). Isaiah finds it in Jerusalem's officials: "All of them love a bribe and run after a payoff" (Isaiah 1:23). Micah lists three offices in order: heads (judges and administrators), priests (who give torah, rulings on what is clean and holy; Deuteronomy 33:10), prophets (who give oracles). The three together are the offices described in Deuteronomy 16:18-18:22. Each now has a price. See the topic Justice.

a: Is the LORD not in the middle of us?
p: A slogan of Zion theology, used by people who cheat; Jeremiah attacks the same confidence.
b: The question is theology, not scorn: "God is inside her; she will not totter" (Psalm 46:5) is the Jerusalem song. The leaders turn it into a promise of safety no matter what they do. Jeremiah answers the same attitude: "Do not trust in lying words. Some people say, 'The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple: that is what these buildings are!'" (Jeremiah 7:4). Micah's reply is the next verse. A God who is in the middle of a people is dangerous to unjust leaders. Amos 5:14 makes the same argument, telling the people that if they seek good they will have the LORD with them, as they claim.

a: Zion will be plowed like a field
p: About a hundred years later, Jeremiah's elders quote this verse and say King Hezekiah repented.
b: Jeremiah 26:17-19 is the most direct use of one prophet's words by another's audience. When Jeremiah was on trial for saying the Temple would fall, elders recalled that Micah had said, "Zion will be plowed like a field. Jerusalem will be heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the house will be high ground in a forest" (Jeremiah 26:18). They add that Hezekiah did not kill Micah; he feared the LORD, and "the LORD changed his mind about the harm" (Jeremiah 26:19). The Hebrew words here and there are the same, so this Plain matches Jeremiah's. The word "Micah" in the Hebrew of Jeremiah is written with the longer spelling Mikhayah and read as Micah. The verse is the earliest identifiable quotation of a prophet in the Bible, if the oracle and its date are as Jeremiah's elders say.

t: The Temple Mount as a wooded height
p: The Temple Mount becomes "high places of a forest": a hilltop of wild growth.
b: "The mountain of the house" is the Temple Mount. Bamot ya'ar means "heights of a forest": the Plain, following Jeremiah, says "high ground in a forest". The same word bamot is used of the hilltop shrines in 1:3 and 1:5. The sentence undoes the Temple's holiness: Zion becomes a plowed field, the city "heaps of rubble" ('iyyim, as in Psalm 79:1), the Temple hill a wood. The scroll 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves the end of this verse, lebamot [ya'ar], and agrees with the Masoretic Text. In 586 BC the Temple was burned (2 Kings 25:9); Lamentations 5:18 sees foxes on Mount Zion.
orig: וְהַר הַבַּיִת לְבָמוֹת יָעַר (vehar habbayit lebamot ya'ar)

p: Hebrew be'acharit hayyamim: "in the aftermath of the days", the future seen from the prophet's own time, sometimes the end.
b: Be'acharit hayyamim is "in the later part of the days" and the phrase has a range. It means "in the days to come" or "in the future" in Genesis 49:1 and Deuteronomy 4:30, and in Numbers 24:14 what Balaam sees for Israel's later history. Hosea 3:5 and Daniel 2:28 give it a larger sense, "in the last days". This Plain follows Isaiah 2:2 here because the Hebrew is the same: "In the days to come". The sense moves between "later time" and "the end"; Jewish and Christian readers have differed on whether the prophets saw a point after which history ends. See the topic The Last Days.
r: Isaiah 2:2; Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14; Deuteronomy 4:30; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 2:28

a: will be set firm at the head of the mountains
p: The same oracle is in Isaiah and Micah, with differences. Who borrowed from whom, or whether both used a third source, is debated.
b: Micah 4:1-3 and Isaiah 2:2-4 are almost word for word the same. Differences: Micah has "peoples" ('ammim) run to the mountain where Isaiah has "all the nations"; Micah says "many nations" go where Isaiah says "peoples in great numbers"; in verse 3 Isaiah says the LORD judges "between the nations" and sets things right for "many peoples", and Micah has the reverse order, with the added words "mighty... however far away". Micah adds a verse (4:4) and a response (4:5); Isaiah ends instead with "House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the LORD's light" (Isaiah 2:5). Views: (1) Isaiah is original and Micah quotes it; (2) Micah is original; (3) both took the oracle from an older source, perhaps a Zion hymn or temple tradition, or from a common editor. The commentaries of Wolff, Mays, Hillers and Allen set out the arguments. The scrolls 4Q82 (4QXIIg) and Mur88 both preserve Micah's "peoples" in 4:1 and agree with the Masoretic Text.

a: like a river, peoples will run to it
p: The verb is "flow like a river"; the picture is of streams of people running uphill, against nature.
b: Naharu comes from nahar, "river". Peoples "river" toward the mountain. A river flows downhill, so the picture is of a river running upward toward the highest point in the land. Isaiah has the same word with "all the nations", and the Plain of Isaiah 2:2 has "like a river, all the nations will run to it". Here the Hebrew has "peoples" and the verb has "upon it" ('alav), not "to it" ('elav) as in Isaiah; the sense is the same. The nations come not as conquerors but as pilgrims: the reverse of 4:11, where the nations gather against Zion.

p: Torah here means "teaching" or "instruction": what the LORD teaches the nations, not only the law of Moses.
b: Torah is "teaching, instruction"; the older "law" is a narrower meaning. This Plain uses "teaching" for the prophet's and the LORD's torah in Isaiah and does the same here, since the nations are said to be taught "from his ways", and "the LORD's word" is in parallel. For a Jewish reader the verse says that the Torah of Sinai has a universal goal; for Christians, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8 describe the word going out "starting from Jerusalem" (Luke 24:47). The scroll 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves 4:2 up to "his paths" and breaks off; Mur88 preserves "For from Zion comes teaching" and the rest, and both agree with the Masoretic Text.
orig: כִּי מִצִּיּוֹן תֵּצֵא תוֹרָה (ki mitsiyyon tetse torah)

a: set things right for mighty nations, however far away
p: The LORD does not conquer the nations here; he decides their disputes. Micah's added words, "mighty" and "far away", widen the audience.
b: Shafat ("judge") is the work of a ruler who decides cases; hokhiach ("set things right") means to decide, rebuke, or arbitrate (Isaiah 11:3-4 has it of the coming king). The LORD is arbiter of nations, so that disputes between them no longer need swords. Micah's words not found in Isaiah are "mighty" ('atsumim) and "however far away" ('ad rachoq): the strong and the far are included. The scroll Mur88 has the words "plowshares" and "pruning knives" beside them and agrees with the Masoretic Text; "mighty" and "far" are restored in it, so it does not decide those two words. See the topic Swords into plowshares.

p: Plowshares cut the soil and pruning knives trim vines; the iron of war becomes the iron of farming. Joel reverses it (Joel 3:10).
b: 'Ittim are the cutting blades of plows (compare 1 Samuel 13:20-21, where only the Philistines had smiths to sharpen them), and mazmerot are pruning knives, hooked blades for the vine. The verb kitet means beat, hammer flat. Hosea 2:18 also pictures bow, sword and war abolished (Hosea 2:18). Joel 3:10 reverses Micah and Isaiah: "Pound your plowshares into swords and your pruning knives into spears." Who borrowed from whom is debated. The Greek translator renders "plows" and "sickles" (see the variant). The Church fathers took this verse as fulfilled in Christ: Justin (First Apology 39) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.34.4) say Christians have already beaten their swords into plows; Origen, answering Celsus, argues from it that Christians do not fight (Against Celsus 5.33). See the card on this verse.

a: beneath a vine of their own
p: Everyone with a vine and a fig tree of their own: the opposite of the land-grabbing of chapter 2.
b: The phrase is a picture of peace and a household's security. Under Solomon, "Judah and Israel stayed safe, everyone sitting under his own vine and his own fig tree" (1 Kings 4:25). The Hebrew has "each man under his vine and under his fig tree". Verse 4 is not in Isaiah's version, and Zechariah 3:10 has the same picture in a later prophet. The image answers chapter 2: where the powerful grab "fields" and "houses" (2:2) and leave poor families without land, this future gives each person a vine, a tree and an unterrified mind. I draw out that link in the chapter's theory box.

p: The title "the LORD of Armies" (YHWH tseva'ot) is used in Micah only here; it seals the oracle.
b: YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (the Plain's rendering throughout, as in Amos 5:15 and Jeremiah 26:18). "Armies" may mean Israel's armies, the angels or the stars; the title sets God at the head of every power. The closing formula, "for the mouth of the LORD of Armies has spoken", is close to the endings of Isaiah 1:20 and 40:5, which read "the mouth of the LORD has spoken" without "of Armies". It is a seal on the promise: the word is as sure as the speaker. This is the only place in Micah that uses the title.
orig: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH tseva'ot), 'the LORD of armies'

p: The Hebrew ki ("for" or "though") gives two readings: all the peoples walk by their gods, but we walk by the LORD.
b: Ki kol ha'ammim yelkhu... ve'anachnu nelekh: the first clause is about the peoples, the second about "us". The Plain reads "For all the peoples walk" because the verse begins with the particle ki, which can mean "for" (the reason for 4:4) or "though" (a concession). Views: (1) A contrast: other peoples have their gods, but we will stay with the LORD whatever others do; (2) a prediction that in the age of peace the nations will still walk after their own gods, while Israel walks with the LORD; (3) a response by the worshipers, like a liturgical vow: the people who hear the oracle answer it. Isaiah's version has a call instead: "House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the LORD's light" (Isaiah 2:5). The Greek (Swete) has no "god" here: it says each people walks "in its own way" (see the variant).

p: The Hebrew ne'um is a noun, "an utterance": the LORD's own declaration.
b: The Hebrew has ne'um YHWH, "an utterance of the LORD". Ne'um is a noun, not a verb: the phrase says "this is the LORD's utterance", and the Plain renders it "the LORD declares", as in 2 Kings 19:33 and 22:19. The prophets use it to mark a sentence as the LORD's own speech, often at the end of an oracle; here it stands inside the line, after "On that day", and gives the promise to gather the lame the weight of a direct word from him.

p: The lame are the weak and scattered people; Jacob himself was lamed at Peniel.
b: Tsole'ah (the lame, the limping) is a word for the weak, and the people of Israel are Jacob, who "limped because of his hip" after wrestling (Genesis 32:31). Zephaniah 3:19 has a close parallel: "I will rescue those who limp and gather those who were driven away." Jeremiah 31:8 puts the blind and the lame in the returning crowd. The point is that the LORD gathers the weakest and the outcast, not the strong. The word niddachah ("driven away", 4:6) is used of the exiled in Deuteronomy 30:4 and Isaiah 11:12; 4:7 uses a different and rarer word, nehla'ah, for "driven far off" (see the variant).

a: the ones I have brought harm to
p: The LORD says he himself did the harm: a rare line where the punishment is owned.
b: The Hebrew ve'asher hare'oti is "and (the one) whom I have harmed". The same root as ra'ah ("harm, evil, disaster") is the word for what the LORD did to his people by exile. The line is unusual in its frankness: the same LORD who scattered now gathers. In Jeremiah 31:28 the LORD says that as he watched to "pluck up and break down... so I will watch to build and plant". The phrase may also be read as the third item in the list: "the lame, the outcast, and those I have harmed".

a: The LORD will be king over them on Mount Zion
p: The kingship of the LORD on Zion is the hope of the psalms and of Isaiah; the remnant becomes a nation.
b: "The LORD will be king" (vemalakh YHWH) answers the question of 4:9 ("Is there no king in you?"). Isaiah 24:23 has "the LORD of Armies will be king on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem", and the royal psalms say "The LORD is king" (Psalm 93:1; 97:1; 99:1). Zechariah 14:9 has the same hope. The "lame" of verse 6 become a "remnant" and the "driven away" a mighty nation (goy 'atsum): the weakest become the strongest. The Hebrew "from now on and forever" (me'attah ve'ad 'olam) is also found in Psalm 113:2 and Psalm 131:3.

p: A tower of the flock, perhaps near Bethlehem and perhaps on the Ophel hill: the first dominion returns to the old royal city.
b: Migdal-eder, "tower of the flock", is a watchtower for shepherds; Jacob camped "beyond Migdal-eder" after Rachel died near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:21). The name here probably refers to a watchtower or to the neighborhood, with 'Ofel, "hill", the Ophel, the spur south of the Temple Mount (2 Chronicles 27:3; Nehemiah 3:26-27). The "tower of the flock" is addressed as "hill of Daughter Zion" and as a symbol of the shepherd-king's city. Readings: a literal tower in Jerusalem; a name for Jerusalem or David's city in a pastoral image; a reference to the area of Bethlehem, to prepare for 5:2. The Greek gives "a dry (or murky) tower of the flock" (see the variant). The Targum of the Minor Prophets, in the Cathcart and Gordon translation, is reported to read the "tower of the flock" as the Messiah of Israel, hidden because of the sins of the congregation of Zion; the Aramaic has not been checked for this scroll.

p: The "first dominion" is the kingdom of David and Solomon restored.
b: Hammemshalah harishonah is "the former rule" or "first dominion". Commentators take it to recall the united kingdom of David and Solomon. The word mamlekhet is "kingdom, kingship"; both nouns are used of the LORD's rule in the Psalms. The Hebrew says the kingship comes "to Daughter Jerusalem". The expectation is that of the Davidic hope (2 Samuel 7:16), and it links to the king from Bethlehem in 5:2. See the topic The Davidic covenant.

a: Is there no king in you?
p: The question may refer to a king lost in 586, a king seized at Jerusalem's gate, or the LORD himself.
b: Readings: (1) A king is gone: Zedekiah, blinded and taken to Babylon in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:7), or the king of Judah in an earlier crisis, such as Sennacherib's siege (701). (2) A sarcastic question: Zion cries as if she had no king, but the LORD is king (4:7). (3) The question is the people's own despair, answered by the promise of verse 7. The "counselor" is the king's adviser (compare Isaiah 9:6, "Wonderful Counselor"). Which view you take depends on whether you place the verses before or after the exile.

a: You will go as far as Babylon.
t: Babylon in the days of Hezekiah?
p: Micah names Babylon, though Assyria was the world power in his time; critics and defenders explain it differently.
b: This is the only time Micah names Babylon. In the late 700s BC Assyria was the empire and Babylon a restless city-state under Assyrian rule. Two main views. (1) Critical: the words come from the exile, after 586 BC, added to the oracle by an editor (for example Wolff and Mays). (2) Conservative: Micah foresaw the exile in Babylon, as his contemporary Isaiah did: Isaiah told Hezekiah that his treasures would be "hauled away to Babylon" (Isaiah 39:6; 2 Kings 20:17), after Merodach-baladan's envoys came. The scroll Mur88 reads "as far as Babylon" here ('ad Bavel), and the Greek has the same. The Hebrew says "you will go as far as Babylon", a place not yet an enemy of Judah. See the topic Babylon.

p: Zion is told to labor like a woman giving birth; the image returns in 5:3.
b: Chuli vegochi means "twist in pain and bring forth." The labor image recurs in prophets for the agony before a new age (Isaiah 26:17-18; Jeremiah 4:31; 30:6). Here the pain of leaving the city, living in the field and traveling to Babylon is the labor from which rescue is born: "There you will be rescued." Verse 9's "pain has seized you like a woman in labor" prepares it. Compare 5:3 ("until she who is in labor has given birth"), in the other part of this book.

p: Chanaf means "be polluted"; the nations want to see Zion defiled.
b: Techenaf is from chanef, "to be polluted, profaned", a word the Old Testament uses for a land defiled by bloodshed (Numbers 35:33; Isaiah 24:5; Jeremiah 3:1-2). In Psalm 79:1 the nations "have made your holy temple unclean". The nations' words (4:11) express hate: they want Zion defiled and gaze on her disgrace. Readers have heard in it the ritual pollution of the Temple (Psalm 79:1), and some hear the shaming of a woman exposed. The Hebrew is "let our eyes gaze on Zion" (vetachaz), a word for looking with pleasure; the Plain says "gloat".

a: gathered them like cut grain onto the threshing floor
p: The nations who gathered against Zion (4:11) are gathered by the LORD like cut grain for threshing.
b: The verb "gather" is qibbets, the same verb the LORD uses of gathering the outcasts in 4:6 (4:11 uses asaf for the nations): the nations gather at Zion, but the LORD is the one who has gathered them, as a farmer brings in sheaves. A threshing floor is where grain is beaten out (Isaiah 21:10; Jeremiah 51:33; Joel 3:13; Amos 1:3). They do not "know the LORD's thoughts" (machshevot): the same word as the "plans" of 2:1 and 2:3. The next verse makes Zion the threshing ox. See the topic Threshing floor.

a: I will make your horn iron
p: Zion becomes a threshing ox; an iron horn is also made by the prophet Zedekiah son of Kenaanah in 1 Kings 22:11.
b: Threshing was done by oxen walking on the grain (Deuteronomy 25:4), and a bull's horns stand for strength: "his horns are a wild ox's horns. With them he will butt the peoples" (Deuteronomy 33:17). Here the ox is Daughter Zion, whose horn is iron and whose hooves are bronze (the metals of weapons and armor). It is the picture of 1 Kings 22:11, where the prophet Zedekiah made himself iron horns to assure King Ahab of victory: "With these you will butt Aram until you finish them off", a false hope that the prophet Micaiah son of Imlah (a name close to Micah's, see 1:2) contradicted. Numbering: the Hebrew Bible's chapter 4 has one more verse than this Plain's; its 4:14 is English 5:1, and from there to the end of chapter 5 the Hebrew numbers run one verse behind the English. Micah's use is the reverse: the strength is the LORD's gift (I will make). The scene shifts from judgment on Judah to victory over the nations.

p: Betsa' is gain taken by violence or fraud; the LORD claims it as his, the way he claimed the spoil of Jericho.
b: Betsa' is gain made by violence or cheating, as in Proverbs 1:19 and Jeremiah 6:13. The verb haram ("set apart for destruction") is the ban of holy war: the spoil of Jericho was set apart for the LORD (Joshua 6:17-19). The words recall chapters 2-3, where the gain of the rich is "stolen" from the poor; here the gain of the nations is given to "the Lord of all the earth". The title "Lord of all the earth" is found in Joshua 3:11 and Psalm 97:5. See the topic Holy war.
